intro.en: Bedside procedures, biopsy techniques, aerosol devices and ward instruments tested in the paediatric practical exam.

items.summary: Needle sampling of spinal fluid through the lower back, used to prove meningitis and to stage leukaemia, but forbidden when pressure inside the skull is raised.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Suspected infection of the brain and coverings (central nervous system infection).
Leukaemia after diagnosis, to rule out spread to the nervous system.
Pseudotumour cerebri (raised pressure with no lump).

blocks.title: Therapeutic uses
bullets: Injecting drugs such as methotrexate for nervous system leukaemia.

blocks.title: Absolute contraindications
bullets: Space occupying lesion inside the skull.
Unequal pupils or unsteady pulse, blood pressure or breathing.
Skin infection over the puncture site.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Downward push of the tonsils with sudden collapse and heart lung arrest.
Carrying skin germs into the spinal fluid space.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: In a traumatic tap every 500 red cells per cubic mm add 1 white cell.
Protein rises by 1 mg/dl for every 1000 red cells per cubic mm.

viva.q: When is lumbar puncture absolutely forbidden?
viva.a: With a space occupying lesion, hydrocephalus, papilloedema, focal signs or low platelets.

viva.q: How do you read a blood stained tap?
viva.a: Allow 1 white cell per 500 red cells and 1 mg/dl protein per 1000 red cells.

viva.q: Name two therapeutic uses of the tap.
viva.a: Methotrexate for nervous system leukaemia and amphotericin for fungal infection.

image.brief: Side view drawing of a child curled on the side with knees drawn up while a thin needle enters the lower spine gap, on a plain background with the needle path marked.

unsure: The book prints '1 ml/dl' for the protein rise, taken as a typo for 1 mg/dl.

items.summary: Reference ranges for healthy spinal fluid in children and newborns, the baseline every meningitis report is judged against.

blocks.title: Normal values
bullets: White cells under 5 per cubic mm in children, up to 10 in the newborn.
Protein 10-40 mg/dl in children, up to 120 mg/dl in the newborn.
Sugar about 60 percent, or two thirds, of blood sugar.

viva.q: What cell count is normal in a child versus a newborn?
viva.a: Under 5 per cubic mm in children, up to 10 in the newborn.

viva.q: How do protein limits differ by age?
viva.a: 10-40 mg/dl in children, up to 120 mg/dl in the newborn.

viva.q: What sugar level is expected?
viva.a: About 60 percent, or two thirds, of blood sugar.

items.summary: Side by side chart separating normal, pyogenic, tuberculous and viral spinal fluid by cells, sugar, protein and special clues.

blocks.title: How to read the chart
blocks.text: Match the dominant cell type first, then check sugar and protein. Low sugar with very high protein points toward tuberculosis; normal sugar with raised cells points toward virus.

head: Condition
Cells
Sugar
Protein
Special clues
rows: Two thirds of random blood sugar
Below two thirds of blood sugar

Cobweb clot; acid fast bacilli on culture
Viral studies; red cells present in herpes

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: N stands for neutrophils and L for lymphocytes in the book chart.
Mumps can lower sugar and herpes can add red cells, unlike other viral cases.

viva.q: How does pyogenic fluid differ from tuberculous fluid?
viva.a: Pyogenic shows neutrophils; tuberculous shows lymphocytes with low sugar and very high protein.

viva.q: What special clue favours tuberculosis?
viva.a: A cobweb clot with acid fast bacilli on culture.

viva.q: Which viral exceptions does the book note?
viva.a: Low sugar in mumps and red cells in herpes.

items.summary: Bedside stomach tube passed through the nose, sized by age and measured from nose to ear to breastbone tip before passing.

blocks.title: Size and length
bullets: Measure from the nose tip to the ear lobe and then to the xiphoid (breastbone tip).

viva.q: How do you measure the tube length?
viva.a: Nose tip to ear lobe, then to the xiphoid process.

viva.q: Which sizes suit a newborn and a young child?
viva.a: 6-8 French for newborns, 12-16 French for young children.

viva.q: Name one diagnostic and one therapeutic use.
viva.a: Gastric aspirate for TB, and tube feeding.

image.brief: Side view of a small child head and chest showing a thin tube path from nose to stomach with the nose to ear to xiphoid measuring points marked, plain background.

items.summary: Needle sampling of liver tissue through the ribs or belly wall to explain enlarged liver, jaundice and storage disorders.

blocks.title: What is done
blocks.text: A needle is passed through the rib cage or the abdominal wall into the liver and a small core is taken for study under the microscope.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Working up an unexplained enlarged liver.
Chronic or repeated conjugated jaundice (raised direct bilirubin).

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Pus pocket (pyogenic abscess) of the liver.
Vascular tumour (angiomatous malformation) of the liver.

blocks.title: Types
bullets: Transjugular biopsy through the neck vein.

viva.q: Name three indications for liver biopsy.
viva.a: Unexplained hepatomegaly, chronic hepatitis and Wilson disease.

viva.q: Which clotting bars stop the biopsy?
viva.a: Prolonged PT or PTT and platelets under 40000 per cubic mm.

viva.q: Name the three techniques.
viva.a: Menghini, Trucut and transjugular.

image.brief: Front view drawing of a child torso with a thin biopsy needle entering the right upper belly below the ribs toward the liver, plain background.

items.summary: The favoured paediatric liver biopsy needle with a 2 cm cutting notch and sleeve, carrying small but real risks of bleeding and organ injury.

blocks.title: Instrument
blocks.text: The book calls it the most used method in children. The needle carries a 2 cm notch with a cutting edge, closed by a sliding sleeve that traps the core.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Blood collection under the capsule or inside the liver.
Bile leak into the chest or belly.

viva.q: Why is the Trucut favoured in children?
viva.a: It is the most used paediatric method, trapping a core in its 2 cm notch.

viva.q: Name three serious complications.
viva.a: Liver haematoma, bile leak and pneumothorax.

viva.q: What does the sleeve do?
viva.a: It slides shut over the notch to cut and trap the tissue core.

image.brief: Close view of a Trucut needle tip showing the open notch and sliding sleeve beside a small tissue core, single instrument on a plain background.

items.summary: Marrow sampling from the back of the hip bone to diagnose blood cancers, marrow failure and storage disorders.

blocks.title: Site and needle
bullets: Site: posterior superior iliac spine of the hip bone.
Needle parts: outer needle, lock and inner stylet.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Needle stopping short of the bony cortex.
Skin death and peeling (necrosis and sloughing) at the site.

viva.q: Where is marrow aspirated in children?
viva.a: The posterior superior iliac spine.

viva.q: Name the needle parts.
viva.a: Outer needle, lock and inner stylet.

viva.q: Name two positioning complications.
viva.a: Stopping short of the cortex and piercing the back cortex.

image.brief: Back view drawing of a child pelvis marking the posterior superior iliac spine puncture point beside a marrow needle with stylet, plain background.

items.summary: Machine that turns liquid medicine into a breathable mist for wheezy children, using compressed air to make droplets 1-5 micrometres wide.

blocks.title: Parts
bullets: Tubing with inlet and outlet joints.
Medicine chamber with cap and jet.

blocks.title: Principle and prescription
bullets: Makes a mixed size mist, mostly droplets 1-5 micrometres, using compressed air.
Add normal saline to reach a total of 5 ml.

viva.q: What droplet size does a nebulizer aim for?
viva.a: Mostly 1-5 micrometres, made with compressed air.

viva.q: What salbutamol dose goes into the chamber?
viva.a: 0.02 ml/kg up to 1 ml, with saline to 5 ml total.

viva.q: How long does one sitting last?
viva.a: 10-20 minutes.

image.brief: Single tabletop nebulizer set with compressor box, tubing, mask and medicine chamber laid out separately on a plain background, front three quarter view.

items.summary: Pocket puffer that fires one fixed drug dose per press, used with a mask and spacer in small children and alone after 12 years.

blocks.title: What it does
blocks.text: Each press releases a fixed amount of drug as a mist. It suits both sudden wheeze attacks and daily control treatment.

blocks.title: Spacer rules by age
bullets: Under 4 years: use with mask and spacer.

blocks.title: Steps of use
bullets: Shake the inhaler 3-4 times and remove the cap.
Breathe out fully, away from the inhaler.
Grip the mouthpiece between the teeth and seal the lips.
Start a slow breath in, press once at the start, and keep breathing in fully.
Remove the inhaler, hold the breath about 10 seconds, then breathe out.
For a second puff wait 30 seconds, shake again and repeat; then rinse the mouth and note the doses taken.

viva.q: Who needs a spacer with an MDI?
viva.a: Under 4 years with mask and spacer; 4-12 years with spacer.

viva.q: When exactly is the canister pressed?
viva.a: At the start of a slow breath in, then keep breathing in fully.

viva.q: What follows the last puff?
viva.a: Rinse the mouth and record the doses taken.

image.brief: Single metered dose inhaler with cap off beside a spacer tube and small mask on a plain background, side view with parts labelled.

items.summary: Breath switched powder inhaler such as the Rotahaler, worked by the child own breath and used above 4 years of age.

blocks.title: How it differs
bullets: Breath actuated: the child own breath pulls the powder in.
Needs no press and breathe timing, unlike the metered dose inhaler.

viva.q: How does a DPI release its dose?
viva.a: The child breath triggers it; no canister press is needed.

viva.q: Below what age is it avoided?
viva.a: At and below 4 years.

viva.q: Name an example device.
viva.a: Rotahaler.

image.brief: Single Rotahaler type dry powder inhaler with its round capsule chamber open beside one capsule, on a plain background, top three quarter view.

items.summary: Blow test with a mini meter for children above 5 years that warns of an oncoming wheeze attack and tracks asthma control.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Spotting an oncoming attack of wheezing.
Judging outlook and treatment compliance in asthma.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Slide the marker to zero and ask the child to stand.
Ask for a deep breath in, then seal the lips round the mouthpiece.
Ask for one maximal hard blow out.
Repeat 3 times and record the highest reading.

blocks.title: Traffic light zones
bullets: Green zone: above 80 percent of personal best.

blocks.title: Baseline formulae
bullets: Boys: (2.96 x height in cm) minus 110.
Girls: (3.43 x height in cm) minus 178.

viva.q: Above what age is PEFR used, and which reading counts?
viva.a: Above 5 years; the highest of 3 blows.

viva.q: What do the three colour zones mean?
viva.a: Green above 80 percent, yellow 50-80, red below 50.

viva.q: How is baseline PEFR estimated for a boy?
viva.a: (2.96 x height in cm) minus 110.

image.brief: Child standing and blowing into a handheld peak flow meter with the marker scale clearly visible, side view on a plain background.

items.summary: Slender 1 cc syringe with a white plastic or metal piston, kept for skin tests, vaccines, test doses and insulin.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: White piston in plastic types, metal piston in glass types.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Giving PPD (purified protein derivative) for the Mantoux test.
Giving test doses such as penicillin.

viva.q: How do you recognise a tuberculin syringe?
viva.a: A 1 cc syringe with a white plastic or metal piston.

viva.q: Which two vaccines or tests use it?
viva.a: PPD for Mantoux and BCG vaccine.

viva.q: Why is it chosen for insulin?
viva.a: Its small 1 cc barrel measures tiny doses exactly.

image.brief: Single 1 cc tuberculin syringe with fine markings and white piston lying beside its needle on a plain background, close side view.

items.summary: Flat L shaped metal or wooden blade that holds the tongue down to expose the throat, tonsils and gag reflex.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Flat L shaped blade of metal or wood.

viva.q: What is a tongue depressor made of?
viva.a: A flat L shaped blade of metal or wood.

viva.q: What four things does it help examine?
viva.a: Pharynx, oral cavity, tonsils and gag reflex.

image.brief: Single L shaped metal tongue depressor beside a wooden disposable one on a plain background, top view with the angled end visible.
